newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - French banks cut lending rates post-budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - French banks cut lending rates post-budget.

text.p: France's leading commercial banks said on Friday they were cutting base lending rates, providing a largely psychological fillip for government attempts to fire up the sluggish economy.

A string of big banks announced that they were cutting base rates, which apply to a relatively small portion of borrowing in France, by 0.20 percent to 6.55 percent, after Thursday's cut in the official intervention rate and falling money market rates.

The move is expected to have a very limited direct impact on the economy but amounted to a further vote of confidence in the wake of the 1997 budget presentation by Prime Minister Alain Juppe's centre-right government on Wednesday.
Banque Nationale de Paris (BNP), Societe Generale, CCF and Credit Lyonnais all said they were cutting their base lending rates to 6.55 percent from 6.75 percent effective Monday.

The base rate is the rate at which banks lend to their best customers but rates to other clients usually follow in the same direction making it generally cheaper for French companies and consumers to borrow money.

Economists said that even if the move was limited, it was one more boost that could bolster consumer and corporate morale and eventually deliver the consumption and investment rise which the government was counting on.
"It's more symbolic than effective on the economy," said ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard in Paris.
Base lending rates applied to a relatively limited amount of funding, he noted. "(But) certainly it's a positive factor."
"It's part of the overall spirit of saying the budget is the way forward," said Sean Shepley, economist at CS First Boston.

After the budget presentation on Wednesday, there was a vote of confidence from the central bank with the intervention rate cut and, now, the commercial banks were adding their weight to the message of hope, he said.
"It has the feel of a concerted attempt to make people feel things are getting better," said London-based Shepley. "All the same, there are genuine prospects for a growth pick-up."
France's independent central bank cut the intervention rate to 3.25 percent from 3.35 percent in an apparent sign of approval of the goverment's 1997 austerity budget.
Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet said the rate cut had been made possible by a slowdown in inflation and by a recovery of the franc on the foreign exchanges.
